title: "Set 11 — hierarchical clustering"
subtitle: "After lecture 12 · 9 November · about 35 minutes"
---

Data: `swiss`, built into R, so there is nothing to download. 47 French-speaking
provinces of Switzerland around 1888: read them as 47 health districts. Six
columns, all percentages or indices (`?swiss` has the details):

| Column | What |
|---|---|
| `Fertility` | a standardised fertility index: higher, more births |
| `Agriculture` | % of men working in farming |
| `Examination`, `Education` | two measures of schooling among army draftees |
| `Catholic` | % Catholic, as opposed to Protestant |
| `Infant.Mortality` | % of live births who die within a year |

```r
Z <- scale(swiss)   # very different spreads: scale first
d <- dist(Z)
```

The Blackboard test checks your numbers against these two lines and the code
below.

## 1 · Four linkages, four trees

Cluster `d` with `complete`, `average`, `single` and `ward.D2`, and plot the four
dendrograms, for instance `plot(hclust(d, method = "single"))`. With 47
provinces the names on the leaves are readable.

One of them produces a long thin tree, with provinces joining one at a time.
Name it, and explain the mechanism that causes it. Cut it at `k = 4` with
`cutree`: which provinces does it leave on their own, and what makes them odd?

## 2 · Cut, and compare

Cut the Ward tree at `k = 3` and profile the groups, back in the original units:

```r
hw <- hclust(d, method = "ward.D2")
groups <- cutree(hw, k = 3)
aggregate(swiss, list(group = groups), mean)   # one row per group
```

Name each group in a few words a health authority would understand. One column
barely changes from one group to the next: which, and what does that mean for
anyone hoping to use these groups to target infant mortality?

Then cross-tabulate against k-means on the same scaled data: `set.seed(11)`,
then `km <- kmeans(Z, 3, nstart = 25)`, then `table(groups, km$cluster)`. The
labels are arbitrary, so match each Ward group with the k-means group it
overlaps most. How many provinces do the two methods place together? Where they
disagree, is it a few provinces on a boundary or an entire group split
differently? Look the disagreeing provinces up in `swiss`: what do they have in
common?

## 3 · The height axis means something

On the Ward dendrogram, find the two largest jumps in merge height:
`rev(hw$height)` lists the merges from the top of the tree down.

What would cutting at each of them give you, and which cut would you defend?
Why is a large jump evidence, and what is the argument it is *not* proof?

## 4 · When the tree is the deliverable [In class]{.badge-class}

[We discuss this one in lecture 13, on 13 Nov — bring your answer.]{.muted}

Hierarchical clustering gives you a nested structure that k-means cannot.

Describe one question, for a health authority or a business, where the
*nesting* is the answer — where knowing that group A splits into A1 and A2
changes a decision — and one where the flat partition is all anybody needs.
